question.text:
\[ P= \begin{bmatrix} 0.9 & 0.2 & 0.3 \\ 0.1 & 0.2 & 0.1 \\ 0 & 0.6 & 0.6 \end{bmatrix}, \qquad \mathbf{q}= \begin{bmatrix} {a} \\ {b} \\ {c} \end{bmatrix} \]

Given that $\mathbf{q}$ is the steady-state vector of the stochastic matrix $P$ shown above, what is the value of $a+b-c?$
question.explanation:
Recall that a steady-state vector of a stochastic matrix $P$ is a stochastic vector $\mathbf{q}$ such that

\begin{align*} P\mathbf{q} &= \mathbf{q} \\[3pt] P\mathbf{q} - \mathbf{q} &= \mathbf{0} \\[3pt] P\mathbf{q} - I\mathbf{q} &= \mathbf{0} \\[3pt] (P - I)\mathbf{q} &= \mathbf{0}. \end{align*}

Computing $P-I,$ we get

\[ P-I = \begin{bmatrix} 0.9 & 0.2 & 0.3 \\ 0.1 & 0.2 & 0.1 \\ 0 & 0.6 & 0.6 \end{bmatrix} - \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} -0.1 & 0.2 & 0.3 \\ 0.1 & -0.8 & 0.1 \\ 0 & 0.6 & -0.4 \end{bmatrix}. \]

The matrix equation $(P-I)\mathbf{q} = \mathbf{0}$ is equivalent to the system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M,$ which we reduce to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination as follows:

\begin{align*} M &= \left[ \begin{array}{ccc|c} -0.1 & 0.2 & 0.3 & 0 \\ 0.1 & -0.8 & 0.1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0.6 & -0.4 & 0 \end{array} \right] && \begin{array}{l} R_1 := 10R_1 \\ R_2 := 10R_2 \\ R_3 := 10R_3 \\ \end{array} \\[5pt] &\sim \left[ \begin{array}{ccc|c} -1 & 2 & 3 & 0 \\ 1 & -8 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 6 & -4 & 0 \end{array} \right] && \begin{array}{l} R_2 := R_2 +R_1 \\ \end{array} \\[5pt] &\sim \left[ \begin{array}{ccc|c} -1 & 2 & 3 & 0 \\ 0 & -6 & 4 & 0 \\ 0 & 6 & -4 & 0 \end{array} \right] && \begin{array}{l} R_3 := R_3 +(-1)R_2 \\ \end{array} \\[5pt] &\sim \left[ \begin{array}{ccc|c} -1 & 2 & 3 & 0 \\ 0 & -6 & 4 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 \end{array} \right] \end{align*}

The reduced matrix above has two pivot columns (the $1$st and $2$nd). Thus, $x_3$ is a free variable. From the second equation, we obtain \[ x_2=\dfrac{2}{3}x_3. \] Substituting this into the first equation, we obtain \[ -x_1+2\left(\dfrac{2}{3}x_3\right)+3x_3 = 0 \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad x_1=\dfrac{13}{3}x_3. \] Hence, the general solution is

\[ \begin{bmatrix} \dfrac{13}{3}x_3 \\ \dfrac{2}{3}x_3 \\ x_3 \end{bmatrix}, \qquad x_3 \in \mathbb{R}. \]

Since the steady-state vector must be stochastic, its entries should add up to $1.$ Therefore, we have

\begin{align*} \dfrac{13}{3}x_3 + \dfrac{2}{3}x_3+x_3 &= 1 \\[5pt] 6x_3 &= 1 \\[5pt] x_3 &= \dfrac{1}{6}. \end{align*}

Therefore,

\[ \mathbf{q}= \begin{bmatrix} a \\ b \\ c \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} \dfrac{13}{18} \\ \dfrac{1}{9} \\ \dfrac{1}{6} \end{bmatrix}. \]

Finally,

\[ a+b-c=\dfrac{13}{18}+\dfrac{1}{9}-\dfrac{1}{6} = \dfrac{2}{3}. \]

example.title: Finding the Steady-State Vector of a Stochastic 3x3 Matrix

question.text:
A particular town has a fleet of $720$ bicycles for rent. The table below gives the pattern of rental and return locations over a typical day.

From:
Museum Station Gym
To: Museum $0.9$ $0.3$ $0.1$
Station $0$ $0.3$ $0.7$
Gym $0.1$ $0.4$ $0.2$

For example, $40\%$ of the bicycles at the Station are moved to the Gym every day.

How many bicycles would eventually be located at the Station if the listed probabilities remained constant over many days?
question.explanation:
From the table, we get the corresponding stochastic matrix

\[ P= \begin{bmatrix} 0.9 & 0.3 & 0.1 \\ 0 & 0.3 & 0.7 \\ 0.1 & 0.4 & 0.2 \end{bmatrix}. \]

Notice that the matrix $P^2$ contains only positive entries. So, the matrix $P$ is regular. As a result, after many years, the distribution will eventually converge to the steady-state vector of $P,$ and this convergence does not depend on the initial state.

Recall that a steady-state vector of a stochastic matrix $P$ is a stochastic vector $\mathbf{q}$ such that

\begin{align*} P\mathbf{q} = \mathbf{q} \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad (P - I)\mathbf{q} = \mathbf{0}. \end{align*}

Computing $P-I,$ we get

\[ P-I = \begin{bmatrix} 0.9 & 0.3 & 0.1 \\ 0 & 0.3 & 0.7 \\ 0.1 & 0.4 & 0.2 \end{bmatrix} - \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} -0.1 & 0.3 & 0.1 \\ 0 & -0.7 & 0.7 \\ 0.1 & 0.4 & -0.8 \end{bmatrix}. \]

The matrix equation $(P-I)\mathbf{q} = \mathbf{0}$ is equivalent to the system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M,$ which we reduce to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination as follows:

\begin{align*} M &= \left[ \begin{array}{ccc|c} -0.1 & 0.3 & 0.1 & 0 \\ 0 & -0.7 & 0.7 & 0 \\ 0.1 & 0.4 & -0.8 & 0 \end{array} \right] && \begin{array}{l} R_1 := 10R_1 \\ R_2 := 10R_2 \\ R_3 := 10R_3 \\ \end{array} \\[5pt] &\sim \left[ \begin{array}{ccc|c} -1 & 3 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & -7 & 7 & 0 \\ 1 & 4 & -8 & 0 \end{array} \right] && \begin{array}{l} R_3 := R_3 +R_1 \\ \end{array} \\[5pt] &\sim \left[ \begin{array}{ccc|c} -1 & 3 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & -7 & 7 & 0 \\ 0 & 7 & -7 & 0 \end{array} \right] && \begin{array}{l} R_3 := R_3 +R_2 \\ \end{array} \\[5pt] &\sim \left[ \begin{array}{ccc|c} -1 & 3 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & -7 & 7 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 \end{array} \right] \end{align*}

The reduced matrix above has two pivot columns (the $1$st and $2$nd). Thus, $x_3$ is a free variable. From the second equation, we obtain \[ x_2=x_3. \] Substituting this into the first equation, we obtain \[ -x_1+3\left(x_3\right)+x_3 = 0 \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad x_1=4x_3. \] Hence, the general solution is

\[ \begin{bmatrix} 4x_3 \\ x_3 \\ x_3 \end{bmatrix}, \qquad x_3 \in \mathbb{R}. \]

Since the steady-state vector must be stochastic, its entries should add up to $1.$ Therefore, we have

\begin{align*} 4x_3 + x_3+x_3 &= 1 \\[5pt] 6x_3 &= 1 \\[5pt] x_3 &= \dfrac{1}{6}. \end{align*}

Therefore,

\[ \mathbf{q} = \begin{bmatrix} \dfrac{2}{3} \\ {\color{blue}{\dfrac{1}{6}}} \\ \dfrac{1}{6} \end{bmatrix}. \]

So, after many days, ${\color{blue}{\dfrac{1}{6}}}$ of the bicycles will be at the station. Therefore, the total number of bikes at the station after many days will be

\[ \dfrac{1}{6} \cdot 720 = 120. \]

example.title: Finding the Steady-State Vector of a Stochastic 3x3 Matrix

question.text:
\[ P= \begin{bmatrix} 0.5 & 0.3 & 0 \\[3pt] 0.35 & 0.45 & 0.6 \\[3pt] 0.15 & 0.25 & 0.4 \end{bmatrix}, \qquad \mathbf{q}= \begin{bmatrix} \dfrac{18}{65} \\[3pt] \dfrac{30}{65} \\[3pt] \dfrac{17}{65} \end{bmatrix} \]

Consider the stochastic matrix $P$ and vector $\mathbf{q}$ shown above. Which of the following statements are true?

  1. $\mathbf{q}$ is a stochastic vector
  2. $P\mathbf{q} = \mathbf{q}$
  3. $\mathbf{q}$ is a steady-state vector of $P$
question.choice2: None of the statements are true
question.explanation:
Recall that a steady-state vector of a stochastic matrix $P$ is a stochastic vector $\mathbf{q}$ such that $P\mathbf{q} = \mathbf{q}.$

With that in mind, let's examine our statements.

  • Statement I is true. Indeed, $\mathbf{q}$ is a stochastic vector since its entries are non-negative and add up to $1.$

  • Statement II is true. Indeed, we have \[ P\mathbf{q} = \begin{bmatrix} 0.5 & 0.3 & 0 \\[3pt] 0.35 & 0.45 & 0.6 \\[3pt] 0.15 & 0.25 & 0.4 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} \dfrac{18}{65} \\[3pt] \dfrac{30}{65} \\[3pt] \dfrac{17}{65} \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} \dfrac{9}{65} + \dfrac{9}{65} + 0 \\[3pt] \dfrac{6.3}{65} + \dfrac{13.5}{65} + \dfrac{10.2}{65} \\[3pt] \dfrac{2.7}{65} + \dfrac{7.5}{65} + \dfrac{6.8}{65} \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} \dfrac{18}{65} \\[3pt] \dfrac{30}{65} \\[3pt] \dfrac{17}{65} \end{bmatrix} = \mathbf{q}. \]

  • Statement III is true. Indeed, $\mathbf{q}$ is a stochastic vector such that $P\mathbf{q}=\mathbf{q}.$ So, it's a steady-state vector of $P.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I, II, and III."

example.title: Identifying Steady-State Vectors of Stochastic Matrices

question.text:
\[ P= \begin{bmatrix} 0.25 & 0.6 \\ 0.75 & 0.4 \end{bmatrix}, \qquad \mathbf{q}= \begin{bmatrix} {a} \\ {b} \end{bmatrix} \]

Given that $\mathbf{q}$ is the steady-state vector of the stochastic matrix $P,$ what is the value of $a-b?$
question.explanation:
Recall that a steady-state vector of a stochastic matrix $P$ is a stochastic vector $\mathbf{q}$ such that

\begin{align*} P\mathbf{q} &= \mathbf{q} \\[5pt] P\mathbf{q} - \mathbf{q} &= \mathbf{0} \\[5pt] P\mathbf{q} - I\mathbf{q} &= \mathbf{0} \\[5pt] (P - I)\mathbf{q} &= \mathbf{0}. \end{align*}

Computing $P-I,$ we get

\[ P-I = \begin{bmatrix} 0.25 & 0.6 \\ 0.75 & 0.4 \end{bmatrix} - \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} -0.75 & 0.6 \\ 0.75 & -0.6 \end{bmatrix}. \]

The matrix equation $(P-I)\mathbf{q} = \mathbf{0}$ is equivalent to the system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M,$ which we reduce to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination as follows:

\begin{align*} M &= \left[ \begin{array}{cc|c} -0.75 & 0.6 & 0 \\ 0.75 & -0.6 & 0 \end{array} \right] & R_2 & := R_2 + R_1 \\[5pt] &\sim \left[ \begin{array}{cc|c} -0.75 & 0.6 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \end{array} \right] \end{align*}

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, $x_2$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain \begin{align} -0.75x_1 + 0.6x_2 & = 0\\[5pt] 75x_1 - 60x_2 & = 0\\[5pt] 5x_1 - 4x_2 & = 0\\[5pt] x_1 & = \dfrac{4}{5}x_2 \end{align}

Hence, the general solution is \[ \begin{bmatrix} \dfrac{4}{5}x_2 \\ x_2 \end{bmatrix}, \qquad x_2 \in \mathbb{R}. \]

Since the steady-state vector must be stochastic, its entries should add up to $1.$ Therefore, we have

\begin{align*} \dfrac{4}{5}x_2 + x_2 & = 1 \\[5pt] \dfrac{9}{5}x_2 & = 1 \\[5pt] x_2 &= \dfrac{5}{9}. \end{align*}

Therefore,

\[ \mathbf{q}= \begin{bmatrix} a \\ b \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} \dfrac{4}{9} \\ \dfrac{5}{9} \end{bmatrix}. \]

Finally, $a - b = \dfrac{4}{9} - \dfrac{5}{9} = -\dfrac{1}{9}.$

example.title: Finding the Steady-State Vector of a Stochastic 2x2 Matrix

question.text:
A factory produces two types of sugar: brown and extra-refined. Every year, the factory's sales executives study how customers' preferences change between the two types of sugar. The table below shows the results of this study.

From:
Brown Extra-Refined
To: Brown $0.8$ $1$
Extra-Refined $0.2$ $0$

It's found that $20 \%$ of customers who currently buy brown sugar will switch to extra-refined sugar next year, while $100 \%$ of customers who currently purchase extra-refined sugar will switch to brown sugar next year.

Assuming that there are $450\,000$ customers in total and that the given probabilities remain constant over many years, how many customers will eventually consume extra-refined sugar?
question.explanation:
From the table, we get the corresponding stochastic matrix \[ P= \begin{bmatrix} 0.8 & 1 \\ 0.2 & 0 \end{bmatrix}. \]

Now, note that \[ P^2 = \begin{bmatrix} 0.84 & 0.8 \\ 0.16 & 0.2 \end{bmatrix}. \]

The matrix $P^2$ contains only positive entries. So, the matrix $P$ is regular. As a result, after many years, the distribution will eventually converge to the unique steady-state vector of $P,$ and this convergence does not depend on the initial state.

Recall that a steady-state vector of a stochastic matrix $P$ is a stochastic vector $\mathbf{q}$ such that

\begin{align*} P\mathbf{q} = \mathbf{q} \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad (P - I)\mathbf{q} = \mathbf{0}. \end{align*}

Computing $P-I,$ we get

\[ P-I = \begin{bmatrix} 0.8 & 1 \\ 0.2 & 0 \end{bmatrix} - \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} -0.2 & 1 \\ 0.2 & -1 \end{bmatrix}. \]

So, the matrix equation $(P-I)\mathbf{q} = \mathbf{0}$ is equivalent to the system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M,$ which we reduce to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination as follows:

\begin{align*} M &= \left[ \begin{array}{cc|c} -0.2 & 1 & 0 \\ 0.2 & -1 & 0 \end{array} \right] & R_2 & := R_2 + R_1 \\[5pt] &\sim \left[ \begin{array}{cc|c} -0.2 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \end{array} \right] \end{align*}

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, $x_2$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain \begin{align} x_1 = 5x_2. \end{align}

Hence, the general solution is \[ \begin{bmatrix} 5x_2 \\ x_2 \end{bmatrix}, \qquad x_2 \in \mathbb{R}. \]

Since the steady-state vector must be stochastic, its entries should add up to $1.$ Therefore, we have \begin{align*} 5x_2 + x_2 & = 1 \\[5pt] 6x_2 & = 1 \\[5pt] x_2 & = \dfrac{1}{6}. \end{align*}

Therefore, \[ \mathbf{q} = \begin{bmatrix} \dfrac{5}{6} \\ {\color{blue}{\dfrac{1}{6}}} \end{bmatrix}. \]

So, ${\color{blue}{\dfrac{1}{6}}}$ of the customers will eventually use extra-refined sugar. Therefore, the number of customers who will eventually use this type of sugar is \[ \dfrac{1}{6} \cdot 450\,000 = 75\,000. \]
